title: Vertical Surfaces & Random Groups
subtitle: Students think at standing whiteboards in randomly assigned groups — one of the highest-impact, lowest-cost changes to how a task lesson runs.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Liljedahl, Building Thinking Classrooms in Mathematics (2020) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014).

blocks.text: Students work on **vertical non-permanent surfaces (VNPS)** — wall whiteboards, windows, or cheap shower-board panels — in **visibly random groups** of two or three, formed fresh in front of the class.

It comes from Peter Liljedahl’s *Building Thinking Classrooms*, which tested dozens of classroom variables and found these two among the most powerful. Standing, erasable, and visible changes student behavior immediately; random grouping breaks the social patterns that let some students hide and others dominate.

Compared with students seated at desks with notebooks, students at vertical whiteboards **start sooner, discuss more, erase and try again instead of stalling, and persist longer**. “Non-permanent” (erasable) lowers the risk of a wrong start; “vertical” makes every group’s thinking visible — to peers and to the teacher monitoring the room. Ideas travel between boards.

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Support productive struggle
Facilitate meaningful discourse
Implement tasks that promote reasoning

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Productive disposition
Strategic competence
Adaptive reasoning

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Groups of 2–3 standing and writing, one marker per group
Students starting within seconds, erasing and retrying
Groups glancing at other boards and borrowing ideas
The teacher circulating, seeing all thinking at once
Random groups that mix who works with whom

no.title: We should not see
items: One student writing while others watch (give one marker, rotate it)
Self-selected friend groups or fixed ability groups
Students seated, copying quietly into notebooks
Boards so spread out the teacher can’t scan the room
Perfectionism — remind them it erases

blocks.title: Two details that make or break it

blocks.text: **(1) One marker per group** — it forces talk and rotation; with three markers you get three kids working alone at the same board. **(2) Groups must be VISIBLY random** (draw cards/names in front of them) — if students suspect the teacher is stacking groups, the status-leveling effect disappears.

items: **Random grouping disrupts status hierarchies** — over weeks, every student works with every other, and “who’s smart at math” stops being fixed.
**Vertical + visible** lets you spot a struggling group instantly and get there before they shut down — access support in real time.
**One marker, rotating,** guarantees every student holds the pen and contributes, including students who’d otherwise defer.
**Erasable** lowers the stakes for students with math anxiety — a wrong start costs nothing.

blocks.text: You don’t need a renovation. Shower board from a hardware store cuts into class-set panels for a few dollars each; windows and existing wall whiteboards work today. Start with one task a week at the boards.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Liljedahl, Building Thinking Classrooms (2020) · Smith & Stein, 5 Practices (2011).

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson

It’s the **structure** for the Explore part of a task lesson — where students work a rich task or a thin-sliced sequence. It pairs with the 5 Practices (you monitor the boards) and Talk Moves (the groups talk).

items: **Form visibly random groups** of 2–3 — draw cards or use a randomizer in front of the class, every time. New groups each task.
**Send them to the boards** — assign each group a vertical surface.
**One marker per group.** The person holding it writes only what the group agrees on; rotate it so everyone takes a turn as scribe.
**Give the task verbally or with a quick visual** — minimal written directions, so the thinking happens at the board, not on a worksheet.
**Step back.** Let them start. Resist explaining; let the struggle begin.

blocks.text: Managing the room while they work

yes.title: Teacher moves
items: Circulate constantly; scan all boards from the center
Use the 5 Practices monitoring grid as you walk
Ask, don’t tell: “What have you tried?” “Why does that work?”
Point a stuck group toward a neighboring board
Use “When to Tell” to decide when to step in

no.title: Watch for
items: One student dominating the marker — rotate it
Groups finishing early — have an extension/sequel ready
Groups stalling — a hint, not the answer
Boards too quiet — prompt a talk move

blocks.text: Groups won’t finish together — that’s fine. Keep a **sequel/extension question** ready for fast groups (“now what if…”), and let slower groups borrow ideas by glancing at other boards (this is a feature, not cheating). You don’t need everyone “done” to consolidate — you need enough thinking to select from.

When there’s enough thinking on the boards, gather the class and run the **Connect** step of the 5 Practices: select 3–4 boards, sequence them, and tie the strategies to the formal mathematics and the learning goal. The boards stay up as a record while you discuss.

items: **Re-randomize every task** — the equity payoff comes from students working across the whole class over time, not from one good grouping.
**Vertical visibility = early help.** You can reach a struggling group before they disengage, which matters most for students who give up quietly.
**Pair with sentence stems** at the boards for multilingual learners, and let gesture and the drawing carry meaning while language develops.

blocks.text: Vertical surfaces and random groups are the physical home of every task-based routine — rich tasks, thin-slicing, and the 5 Practices all run here. Establish the structure once and it powers the whole Core.
